MECH 420 · Mechanical Design I · Chapter 11

Rolling-Contact Bearings

Section 11–1, bearing types: what the eight common bearings look like inside, which loads each one carries, and how to choose between them.

Based on Shigley’s Mechanical Engineering Design, 11th ed., and B. Zoghbi’s lecture slides.

Deep-groove ballAngular-contact ballSelf-aligning ballThrust ballCylindrical rollerSpherical rollerTapered rollerNeedle roller

11–1 · Ball or roller?

The contact decides capacity and speed

A rolling bearing carries its load through rolling, not sliding. Starting friction is only about twice running friction, which is negligible next to a sleeve bearing. Every rolling bearing is either a ball or a roller bearing.

BallRoller
ContactPointLine
Load capacity, same sizeLowerHigher
Speed limitHigherLower
FrictionLowerHigher
Cost, small sizesLowerHigher

A ball touches the raceway at a point that flattens into a tiny ellipse; a roller touches along a line that flattens into a long strip. More contact area means lower contact (Hertz) stress for the same load, so a higher load rating. Shigley: “Straight roller bearings will carry a greater radial load than ball bearings of the same size because of the greater contact area.” The longer contact also means more friction and heat, which limits speed.

11–1 · Nomenclature · Fig. 11–1

Four parts: two rings, rolling elements, a cage

The outer ring usually sits in the housing; the inner ring is pressed onto the shaft and turns with it. The balls roll in grooves called raceways. The separator, which catalogs call the cage or retainer, keeps the balls evenly spaced so they don’t rub on each other. Catalogs size a bearing by its bore, outside diameter and width. In the animation at the top of the page the cage carries the balls round at a little under half the shaft speed.

11–1 · The eight types

What each bearing carries

Each drawing is a half-section above the shaft centreline. Orange arrows are loads the bearing carries; grey arrows are loads it can’t. The dashed orange line is the line of contact through the rolling element. Press Replay loads to see the radial load, then the axial load.

Ball bearing · point contact · Fig. 11–2a

Deep-groove ball bearing

Deep grooves in both rings hold the ball from both sides: radial load plus moderate thrust either way.

Radial loadModerate
Axial loadModerate, both directions
SpeedVery high (low friction)
Allowable slope0.001–0.003 rad (Table 7–2)

Use it for: electric motors, fans, small gearboxes. The default choice: cheap, sealed, needs little maintenance.

From Shigley: the balls are inserted by moving the inner ring to an eccentric position; the separator goes in afterward. A filling-notch version (Fig. 11-2b) fits more balls, so more radial capacity, but less thrust capacity because balls bump the notch edge. Shields (11-2d) keep out dirt but are not a full closure; sealed bearings (11-2e) are lubricated at the factory. The dashed orange line is the line of contact: under pure radial load it runs straight through the ball. Because the groove rises on both sides of the ball, a thrust from either direction pushes the ball against a groove wall, and the contact line tilts to carry it. That is why this one type covers most light-to-moderate applications. Friction is low, so it runs fast. Sealed and shielded versions come pre-greased and need essentially no maintenance.

Ball bearing · point contact at an angle · Fig. 11–2c

Angular-contact ball bearing

One shoulder of each ring is cut low, so the load passes through the ball at a contact angle α. Tilting the contact line lets it carry heavy thrust, but only from one side.

Radial loadModerate
Axial loadHigh, one direction
SpeedHigh
Allowable slopeLow

Use it for: machine-tool spindles, pumps, worm-gear shafts. Usually mounted in pairs so thrust is taken both ways.

Follow the dashed line: the high left shoulder of the inner ring pushes the ball up and to the right, into the high right shoulder of the outer ring. So a thrust pushing the shaft to the right is carried. Push the shaft to the left and the low shoulders let the ball walk out; nothing carries that load. That is why angular-contact bearings are almost always used in pairs, or opposed by a second bearing at the other end of the shaft. A larger contact angle means more thrust capacity and less radial capacity.

Ball bearing · two rows, spherical outer race · Fig. 11–2h

Self-aligning ball bearing

The outer raceway is one sphere centred on the shaft axis, so the inner ring and balls can swivel to follow a bent or misaligned shaft.

Radial loadModerate
Axial loadLight
SpeedHigh
Allowable slope0.026–0.052 rad (Table 7–2)

Use it for: long shafts that deflect, housings that can’t be aligned precisely: conveyors, agricultural machinery.

Shigley: single-row bearings withstand a small amount of misalignment or deflection; where it is severe, use self-aligning bearings. Compare the allowable slopes from Table 7-2 in Chapter 7: a deep-groove bearing tolerates about 0.001 to 0.003 rad of shaft slope, a self-aligning bearing 0.026 to 0.052 rad, roughly 20 times more. The trick is the spherical outer raceway: because its centre lies on the shaft axis, tilting the inner ring just rolls the balls to a different spot on the same sphere. The price is that the balls contact a nearly flat sphere on the outside, so thrust capacity is low. If the load is heavy, the roller version of the same idea is the spherical roller bearing.

Ball bearing · contact parallel to the shaft · Fig. 11–2i

Thrust ball bearing

Two grooved washers instead of rings. Contact runs along the shaft: axial load only, in one direction.

Radial loadNone
Axial loadModerate, one direction
SpeedLow to moderate
Allowable slopeVery low

Use it for: vertical shafts, turntables, screw jacks. Pair it with a radial bearing that takes the radial load.

The shaft washer is fitted on the shaft; the housing washer has a larger bore so it clears the shaft and sits against the housing. Push the shaft to the right and the balls are squeezed between the washers. Push it to the left and the washers simply separate, so a single thrust bearing locates the shaft in one direction only. Double-direction versions add a third washer. At high speed, centrifugal force pushes the balls outward in the grooves, which is why speed is limited.

Roller bearing · line contact · Fig. 11–3a

Cylindrical roller bearing

Line contact spreads the load: very high radial rating. Needs near-perfect alignment; a slight tilt skews the rollers.

Radial loadVery high
Axial loadNone (straight rollers)
SpeedHigh
Allowable slope0.0008–0.0012 rad (Table 7–2)

Use it for: gearboxes, motors, rolling mills; the “free” bearing at one end of a shaft that grows with heat.

Shigley: straight roller bearings carry a greater radial load than ball bearings of the same size because of the greater contact area, but they need almost perfect geometry of raceways and rollers; a slight misalignment makes the rollers skew, so the retainer must be heavy, and they will not take thrust. In this sketch only the outer ring has ribs, so the inner ring and shaft can slide axially through the rollers: this is a non-locating (floating) bearing. That is useful at the free end of a shaft whose length changes with temperature, with a locating bearing such as a deep-groove ball bearing at the other end. Versions with ribs on both rings can take some light thrust through roller-end sliding contact. Line contact makes these bearings sensitive to misalignment: note the very small allowable slope from Table 7-2, because a tilted roller loads only one edge.

Roller bearing · two rows, spherical outer race

Spherical roller bearing

Self-aligning, with rollers: barrel rollers on a spherical outer raceway tolerate misalignment and carry heavy loads.

Radial loadVery high
Axial loadModerate, both directions
SpeedModerate
Allowable slopeHigh (self-aligning)

Use it for: heavy machinery that flexes: crushers, vibrating screens, paper-mill rolls, wind-turbine main shafts.

Same principle as the self-aligning ball bearing: the outer raceway is one sphere centred on the shaft axis, so the inner ring with both rows of rollers can tilt. Because the rollers are barrel-shaped and sit at an angle, each row also takes thrust; two opposed rows give moderate thrust in both directions. They are robust and forgiving, at the cost of more friction and lower speed than ball bearings.

Roller bearing · line contact at an angle · Fig. 11–3e

Tapered roller bearing

Conical rollers between a cone and a cup, all pointing to one apex on the shaft axis. Takes any mix of radial and one-way thrust.

Radial loadHigh
Axial loadHigh, one direction
SpeedModerate
Allowable slope0.0005–0.0012 rad (Table 7–2)

Use it for: wheel hubs, gearbox shafts, differentials. Always opposed by a second bearing (next slide).

Shigley 11-1: tapered roller bearings combine the advantages of ball and straight roller bearings: they take radial or thrust load or any combination, with the high capacity of straight roller bearings. They are designed so that all elements of the roller surface and the raceways intersect at a common point on the bearing axis; that is the apex drawn here, and it is why the rollers roll without skidding. The inner ring is called the cone, the outer ring the cup; the cup separates from the cone-and-rollers assembly. Pushing the shaft to the left wedges the cone into the narrowing cup and is carried. Pushing it right just lifts the cone out of the cup, so a single bearing cannot locate the shaft both ways. A steep-angle version (Fig. 11-3f) carries more thrust.

Roller bearing · line contact · Fig. 11–3d

Needle roller bearing

Long, thin rollers in a very thin section; the shaft can be the inner raceway, so it fits where radial space is tight.

Radial loadHigh for its size
Axial loadNone
SpeedModerate
Allowable slopeVery low

Use it for: rocker arms, gearbox planet gears, universal joints, two-stroke connecting rods.

Shigley 11-1: needle bearings are very useful where radial space is limited. They have a high load capacity when separators are used, but may be obtained without separators, and they come both with and without races. When there is no inner race, the shaft itself must be hardened and ground to serve as the raceway. Like other straight rollers they take no thrust, and their long thin rollers make them very sensitive to misalignment.

Tapered roller bearings · mounting

One-way thrust, so they work in pairs

Two opposed bearings each take thrust one way, so together they locate the shaft in both directions. The orange pressure lines show where each bearing’s load acts; where a line meets the shaft axis is that bearing’s effective load centre.

Back-to-back (O): load centres outside the bearings, so the effective span is wider than the bearing spacing and the pair is stiff against tilting moments. Used in wheel hubs and spindles.

Face-to-face (X): load centres between the bearings, so the span is short. Less stiff against moments, but more forgiving of misalignment.

The same two arrangements apply to pairs of angular-contact ball bearings.

The eight types side by side

TypeContactRadialAxialSpeedSlope (rad)Typical use
Deep-groove ballPointModerateModerate, 2 waysVery high0.001–0.003Motors, general

Slopes are from Shigley Table 7–2 (Chapter 7). Ratings are relative, for bearings of similar bore. “1 way” types are used in opposed pairs. Read the table by column: only the angled-contact types carry heavy thrust, and only one way; only the two spherical-raceway types forgive real misalignment; roller types win on capacity and ball types on speed.

more slope for the spherical-raceway types (orange) than for the rigid types (blue). Note the log scale.

Check the shaft slope at each bearing, as in the Chapter 7 shaft-design example. If it exceeds the blue range, stiffen the shaft or switch to a self-aligning type. Spherical roller bearings are not listed in Table 7–2 but are also self-aligning.

Choosing a type

Start from the load and the shaft

Mostly radial, high speed

Deep-groove ball

Heavy radial, no thrust

Cylindrical roller

Radial plus heavy thrust one way

Tapered roller or angular contact, in pairs

Shaft deflects or housings misaligned

Self-aligning ball (light) or spherical roller (heavy)

Pure thrust

Thrust ball

Almost no radial space

Needle roller

Try it: for a car wheel, an electric motor, a drill-press spindle and a conveyor roller, decide which card applies. A real shaft usually has two different bearings: one locating bearing that takes the thrust, and one floating bearing, often a cylindrical roller, that lets the shaft grow with temperature.
